blocks.content: Every routing rule covered so far has quietly assumed plain HTTP. Real production traffic almost never is. This topic covers exactly how Ingress secures every one of those host and path rules with real, working HTTPS.
TLS, Given Its Own Full Depth
blocks.text: TLS, Given Its Own Full Depth

blocks.content: TLS support in Ingress lets a single controller terminate HTTPS encryption for any number of domains, decrypting incoming encrypted traffic and forwarding plain HTTP internally to backend Services, exactly the same termination pattern already introduced for LoadBalancer Services.

This is configured through a tls section in the Ingress manifest, listing which hosts require TLS and which Kubernetes Secret holds the actual certificate and private key to use for encrypting traffic to those specific hosts.

The certificate itself is stored as an ordinary Kubernetes Secret of type kubernetes.io/tls, containing the certificate and its private key as two separate data fields, referenced by name from the Ingress manifest's tls section.

This means certificate management, while requiring its own separate process to actually obtain a valid certificate, integrates directly into the same declarative, version controlled manifest already used for every other piece of Ingress configuration covered in this module.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643083277-428296086.png
blocks.alt: TLS given its own full depth

blocks.content: Termination Happens at the Ingress Controller
blocks.text: Termination Happens at the Ingress Controller

blocks.content: When a client makes an HTTPS request to a domain routed through Ingress, the TLS handshake and decryption happen at the Ingress controller itself, using the certificate referenced in the matching tls entry for that specific hostname.

Once decrypted, the request is forwarded internally to the backend Service as plain HTTP, meaning backend application Pods generally do not need to handle TLS themselves at all, simplifying their own configuration significantly.

This internal, plain HTTP traffic stays entirely within the cluster's own private network, which is the same trust boundary reasoning already established throughout the Services module for why ClusterIP internal traffic does not need its own separate encryption in most cases.

For environments with a stricter security requirement demanding encryption all the way to the backend Pod itself, a service mesh or a per Pod TLS configuration can be layered on top, though this goes beyond what Ingress alone provides by default.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643084878-32503607.png
blocks.alt: TLS terminated right at the Ingress controller

blocks.content: A Real TLS Example

Consider api.example.com, already routed through Ingress in the previous topic's example, now needing to serve HTTPS traffic exclusively, with any plain HTTP request either rejected or automatically redirected to its encrypted equivalent.

A Kubernetes Secret named api-example-tls is created, holding the certificate and private key for api.example.com, and the Ingress manifest's tls section references that Secret by name against that specific host.

Once applied, any HTTPS request to api.example.com is correctly terminated using that certificate, and most Ingress controller implementations automatically redirect any plain HTTP request to its HTTPS equivalent, without requiring any extra configuration.

This single addition to the existing Ingress manifest, without touching the backend Service or Deployment at all, is precisely the kind of clean separation of concerns that makes Ingress a genuinely practical, maintainable way to manage HTTPS across many applications.

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: company-ingress
spec:
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - api.example.com
      secretName: api-example-tls
  rules:
    - host: api.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: api-service
                port:
                  number: 80

blocks.content: Recap: TLS Termination Already Introduced

The LoadBalancer topic in the previous module already introduced TLS termination as a capability, describing a cloud load balancer decrypting HTTPS traffic before forwarding plain HTTP to the cluster, configured through provider specific annotations at the time.

Ingress offers this exact same capability, but with one meaningful improvement: it operates per hostname, letting dozens of different domains each use their own distinct certificate, all managed through the same Ingress manifest and terminated at the same controller.

A LoadBalancer Service's TLS termination, by contrast, is typically scoped to the entire load balancer, making it considerably less convenient for the many domains, one Ingress controller pattern this entire module has been built around.

Recognizing Ingress TLS as a direct, more granular evolution of that earlier LoadBalancer capability, rather than an unrelated new feature, ties this topic cleanly back into everything already established two modules of content ago.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643088018-171507891.png
blocks.alt: Recap of TLS termination at the load balancer, already covered

blocks.content: Automating Certificate Management

Manually obtaining, uploading, and renewing a TLS certificate for every single domain quickly becomes an unmanageable operational burden as the number of domains routed through Ingress grows, particularly since most certificates expire and require renewal every few months.

cert-manager, a widely adopted open source project, automates this entire process, watching Ingress objects for domains needing certificates and automatically requesting, renewing, and storing them as Kubernetes Secrets without any manual intervention required.

cert-manager commonly integrates with Let's Encrypt, a free, automated certificate authority, letting a cluster obtain and continuously renew genuinely valid, publicly trusted certificates for every domain routed through Ingress at effectively zero ongoing cost.

Installing cert-manager alongside an Ingress controller is a strongly recommended practice for any production cluster serving real HTTPS traffic, removing an entire category of manual, error prone, and easily forgotten operational work.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643089583-277683642.png
blocks.alt: An automated certificate tool renewing certificates for every host

blocks.content: A Common Mistake: Letting Certificates Expire
blocks.text: A Common Mistake: Letting Certificates Expire

blocks.content: A genuinely common and genuinely damaging mistake is manually obtaining a TLS certificate once, deploying it correctly, and then never establishing any process to renew it before its typically ninety day or one year expiration date arrives.

An expired certificate causes every browser and HTTP client to reject the connection outright with a clear, user visible security warning, which is precisely the kind of highly visible, trust damaging outage that automated renewal exists specifically to prevent.

This mistake is entirely avoidable through the cert-manager automation covered in the previous section, which is precisely why manual certificate management, without any automated renewal process, is strongly discouraged for any genuine production environment.

Any cluster still relying on manually managed certificates should treat migrating to an automated renewal process, such as cert-manager, as a high priority operational improvement rather than an optional nicety to address eventually.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643091207-369396829.png
blocks.alt: The mistake of letting a TLS certificate expire without automated renewal

blocks.content: Multiple Hosts, Multiple Certificates, One Ingress
blocks.text: Multiple Hosts, Multiple Certificates, One Ingress

blocks.content: A single Ingress object's tls section can list multiple entries, each specifying a different set of hosts and a different Secret, letting one Ingress manifest manage TLS termination for many entirely distinct domains simultaneously.

This directly mirrors the multiple host rules pattern already established in the previous topic, extending that same per domain granularity to certificate management rather than requiring a separate Ingress object for every domain needing its own distinct certificate.

Some certificates, called wildcard certificates, can cover an entire set of subdomains under one domain with a single certificate, reducing the number of distinct certificates that need to be separately requested, stored, and renewed.

Choosing between individual per domain certificates and a broader wildcard certificate is a genuine tradeoff between operational simplicity and the security principle of limiting a single certificate's blast radius if it were ever compromised.

{"headers":["Approach","Tradeoff"],"rows":[["Individual certificates","Smaller blast radius, more certificates to manage"],["Wildcard certificate","Simpler management, larger blast radius if compromised"]]}
How cert-manager Actually Works

cert-manager introduces its own Kubernetes objects, most notably Certificate and Issuer, which describe what certificate is needed and which certificate authority should issue it, continuing the exact same declarative, controller reconciled pattern already familiar throughout this course.

A ClusterIssuer configured for Let's Encrypt performs an automated domain ownership challenge, typically by briefly serving a specific file at a well known path or by creating a temporary DNS record, proving control over the domain before a certificate is issued.

Once issued, cert-manager stores the resulting certificate as an ordinary Kubernetes Secret, exactly the same kind of Secret referenced manually in this topic's earlier real example, meaning no change to the Ingress manifest's tls section is required to adopt it.

cert-manager also tracks each certificate's expiration date continuously, automatically requesting a renewed certificate well before the old one expires, closing the loop on the exact common mistake covered earlier in this topic entirely automatically.
A Real cert-manager Configuration

Installing cert-manager and configuring a ClusterIssuer for Let's Encrypt typically requires only a small number of manifests, applied once per cluster, after which requesting a certificate for any new domain becomes a matter of a single annotation on an Ingress object.

Adding the annotation cert-manager.io slash cluster-issuer with the name of the configured ClusterIssuer to an Ingress object instructs cert-manager to automatically request and manage a certificate for every host listed in that Ingress object's tls section.

From that point forward, the entire certificate lifecycle, initial issuance, ongoing renewal, and Secret management, happens automatically and continuously, with no further manual action required for that domain unless its configuration genuinely needs to change.

This single annotation based workflow is precisely why cert-manager has become the strongly recommended default for TLS management across the overwhelming majority of production Kubernetes clusters running Ingress today.

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: company-ingress
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - api.example.com
      secretName: api-example-tls
  rules:
    - host: api.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: api-service
                port:
                  number: 80

blocks.content: TLS Versions and Cipher Configuration

Beyond simply having a valid certificate, an Ingress controller also determines which TLS protocol versions and cipher suites are actually accepted during the handshake, a configuration surface most controller implementations expose through their own specific annotations or ConfigMap settings.

Modern best practice generally means disabling older, known weak TLS versions such as TLS 1.0 and 1.1, restricting the controller to TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only, which nearly every modern browser and HTTP client already supports without issue.

Most Ingress controller implementations ship with reasonably secure default cipher and version settings out of the box, meaning most teams never need to touch this configuration directly, but security conscious environments should verify these defaults explicitly rather than assuming them.

This is a genuinely good example of security work that mostly happens once, at the controller configuration level, rather than needing to be repeated for every individual application or domain routed through that same controller.
Debugging a Broken TLS Handshake

When a client reports a TLS related connection failure, the first check is confirming the referenced Secret actually exists and contains valid certificate data, using kubectl describe secret to inspect it without exposing the private key itself in plain output.

The second check is confirming the certificate's covered hostnames, known as its Subject Alternative Names, actually include the specific domain the client is attempting to reach, since a mismatched certificate produces a clear, specific browser warning about the wrong domain.

The third check is confirming the certificate has not expired, directly addressing the single most common real world cause of TLS failures covered as this topic's common mistake, and one that automated renewal through cert-manager is specifically designed to prevent.

Working through these three checks in order, Secret existence, hostname coverage, and expiration, resolves the overwhelming majority of real world TLS handshake failures encountered when operating Ingress in production.

{"headers":["Step","What to Check"],"rows":[["1","Secret exists and contains valid certificate data"],["2","Certificate covers the exact hostname being requested"],["3","Certificate has not expired"]]}
Verifying TLS Configuration in Practice

Running kubectl get secret api-example-tls -o yaml confirms the certificate Secret exists and contains both a certificate and a private key field, a useful first check before assuming the Ingress controller is somehow misconfigured.

A direct curl request against the domain, using the verbose flag to inspect the certificate details returned during the TLS handshake, confirms exactly which certificate the Ingress controller is actually presenting to real clients.

Browser developer tools, specifically the security tab available in most modern browsers, provide a genuinely convenient, visual way to inspect a live certificate's issuer, expiration date, and covered domains without needing any command line tooling at all.

Building the habit of checking certificate expiration dates as part of regular, routine cluster health checks, even with automated renewal in place, provides a valuable extra layer of confidence that the renewal automation is genuinely working as expected.
Best Practices for TLS With Ingress
blocks.text: Best Practices for TLS With Ingress

blocks.content: Install cert-manager, or an equivalent automated certificate management tool, on any cluster serving real production HTTPS traffic, rather than relying on manually obtained and manually renewed certificates.

Monitor certificate expiration dates explicitly, even with automation in place, treating any certificate within a short window of expiring as a genuine, actionable alert rather than something to notice only after an outage has already occurred.

Choose between individual and wildcard certificates deliberately, based on a genuine security and operational tradeoff assessment, rather than defaulting to whichever approach happened to be simplest to set up initially.

Test TLS configuration directly with curl or browser developer tools immediately after any change, exactly as recommended for routing rules in the previous two topics, rather than assuming a certificate change took effect correctly.

blocks.content: The Single Most Valuable Takeaway

TLS support in Ingress brings the same per domain granularity already established for routing in the previous two topics to HTTPS certificate management, letting one controller securely terminate encryption for any number of independently managed domains.

Automated certificate management, most commonly through cert-manager and Let's Encrypt, should be treated as a default, near mandatory piece of any production Ingress setup, not an optional enhancement to consider only later.

The next topic, Default Backend, covers what happens to a request that matches none of the host or path rules covered across the last three topics, closing the final gap in a genuinely complete Ingress configuration.

Keep the certificate expiration risk firmly in mind. It is one of the few Ingress related failures that can go completely unnoticed for months, right up until the exact moment it becomes a highly visible, user facing outage.

With routing and security now both fully covered, the final routing focused topic in this module addresses the one remaining gap: what happens to a request that matches none of the rules established across these last three topics.
TLS is now fully covered; Default Backend, the fallback for everything these rules do not match, follows immediately next.

points: Ingress TLS termination decrypts HTTPS at the controller per hostname, using a Kubernetes Secret of type kubernetes.io/tls referenced from the manifest's tls section.

It extends the TLS termination concept already introduced for LoadBalancer Services, but with far finer, per domain granularity suited to the many domains, one controller pattern this module is built around.
cert-manager, paired with Let's Encrypt, is the strongly recommended way to automate certificate issuance and renewal, avoiding the real risk of an expired, user visible certificate outage.
A single Ingress object's tls section can cover multiple hosts and certificates simultaneously, mirroring the multi host routing pattern from the previous topic.
